Commander increments the Node inspector port when spawning an executable subcommand, but the host patterns exclude colons. Bracketed IPv6 hosts therefore bypass the incrementer, and the child tries to use the parent's port.

For example, running `node --inspect=[::1]:19340 tests/fixtures/inspect.js sub` on `develop` prints `Starting inspector on ::1:19340 failed: address already in use`. With this fix, the child starts its inspector on `[::1]:19341`.

Recognise bracketed IPv6 hosts in the existing shared parser, both with an explicit port and with the default port. Add separate regressions for IPv6 hosts with and without an explicit port using the existing executable-subcommand test helper. No dependencies or API changes.

Validation:
- The regression fails before the fix and passes afterward.
- All 1,427 runtime tests and TypeScript tests pass on Node 22.22.0, 24.21.0, and 26.10.0.
- `pnpm check` passes, including JavaScript and TypeScript checks, ESLint, and Prettier.
- The real parent/child reproduction opens separate IPv6 inspector ports after the fix.
- Checked all four supported inspector flags with IPv6, IPv4, hostname, default-port, and port-zero inputs.

## Problem

Executable subcommands already bump the Node inspector port so the child does not collide with the parent. That covers `--inspect` and `--inspect-brk`, but `--inspect-wait` is left as-is.

```
node --inspect-wait app.js cache
```

The child is spawned with the same `--inspect-wait` (port 9229). Node documents `--inspect-wait[=[host:]port]` the same way as `--inspect-brk`; the incrementer should treat it the same.

## Solution

Recognise `--inspect-wait` in `incrementNodeInspectorPort` and rewrite host/port the same way as `--inspect-brk`.

- `--inspect-wait` → `--inspect-wait=127.0.0.1:9230`
- `--inspect-wait=100` → `--inspect-wait=127.0.0.1:101`

## ChangeLog

body:
## Problem

Option variadic detection used `\w`, which only recognises ASCII word characters.

As a result, Unicode placeholders such as `--tag <值...>` were treated as non-variadic options, causing parsing of multiple values to fail with an excess-argument error.

The same issue also affects placeholders whose final identifier character is a Unicode combining mark or connector punctuation, such as decomposed names and the exact reproduction discussed in #2614.

Fixes #2614.

## Solution

Use the Unicode `ID_Continue` property to recognise valid identifier-continuation characters immediately before the variadic ellipsis.

This covers:

- Unicode letters and numbers
- Combining marks
- Connector punctuation
- Existing ASCII word characters

This preserves the existing behaviour for ASCII placeholders while continuing to reject non-variadic or malformed forms such as `<value,...>`, `<...>`, and `<value....>`.

## Tests

Added one regression test alongside the existing variadic special-case tests: a placeholder ending in a decomposed Unicode combining mark (`[cafe\u0301...]`) is recognised as variadic.

The existing `[value,...]` test continues to verify that CSV-like single-argument placeholders are not treated as variadic. I also manually verified that the issue's `<值...>` example collects both values. On Node 22.19.0, the full suite passed (1,405 passed, 4 skipped), along with type, lint, and format checks.

## ChangeLog

- Support Unicode variadic option placeholders, including combining marks and connector punctuation.

Some code and tests were assisted by Codex. I reviewed, understood, and tested the complete change and take responsibility for it.

body:
## Problem

`InvalidOptionArgumentError` has been deprecated since Commander v8 and is documented as such in `docs/deprecated.md`, but nothing tells you that at the use site. It is declared in the typings as a re-export:

```ts
export { InvalidArgumentError as InvalidOptionArgumentError }; // deprecated old name
```

A re-export statement cannot carry a JSDoc comment, so TypeScript and editors have no `@deprecated` tag to act on. Users get no strikethrough and no hover hint — the `// deprecated old name` comment is only visible to somebody reading Commander's own source.

## Solution

Replace the re-export in `typings/index.d.ts` with declarations that can be annotated:

```ts
/** @deprecated since v8, instead use InvalidArgumentError */
export const InvalidOptionArgumentError: typeof InvalidArgumentError;
/** @deprecated since v8, instead use InvalidArgumentError */
export type InvalidOptionArgumentError = InvalidArgumentError;
```

Editors now strike through the identifier and point at `InvalidArgumentError`.

Both halves are needed to stay backwards compatible, because the old re-export put the name in **both** value space and type space:

- Without the `const`, the existing `typings/index.test-d.ts` case `new commander.InvalidOptionArgumentError('message')` fails.
- Without the `type` alias, `let e: InvalidOptionArgumentError` fails with `TS2749: 'InvalidOptionArgumentError' refers to a value, but is being used as a type here`.

The runtime export in `index.js` is unchanged. No runtime or type behaviour changes — this is purely about surfacing the existing deprecation in editors.

`npm run test` and `npm run check` both pass.

## ChangeLog

- add `@deprecated` JSDoc tag to `InvalidOptionArgumentError` typings so editors show the deprecation

## Problem

The option delimiter is stripped during top level pass of arguments by root command before the subcommand sees the arguments. This works for internal subcommands (action handler) because the following arguments are marked as having been processed. This does not work for external subcommands which just get the arguments without the option terminator and following options get processed as normal.

Issue: #2530

Leave the option terminator and the remaining arguments as "unknown" for the subcommand to reprocess. This works for both internal and external commands.

The option terminator tests were weak. Beefed them up to cover the external case and more besides.

This is a change in core behaviour, so marking PR as semver-major.

## Problem

Running fixture loops with embedded tests at top level of `describe` is running the tests at file load time instead of a test time. This is not causing any known problems at the moment, but could cause confusion in the future.

Issue picked up by `node-test/require-hook`:

- https://github.com/sindresorhus/eslint-node-test/blob/main/docs/rules/require-hook.md

## Solution

Wrap fixture loops in a test, and by convention use await for the nested test.

Couple of other tidies:
- use built-in support for conditional test/describe
- remove `node-test/require-top-level-describe` as we often use a top level `test` rather than `describe`, and don't want extra wrapper or to suppress the warning everywhere that pattern used.

The changes are a bit noisy, but a fairly pure refactor. (Turning off whitespace in the diff may help make this clearer.)

body:
Commander accepts unescaped negative numbers as command-arguments and as optional/variadic option-arguments (README: "Negative numbers are special and are accepted as an option-argument"). The negative-number detector matches only a lowercase `e` exponent, so a negative number written with an uppercase `E` (`-1E3`, `-1.2E-3`) is not recognised and is rejected as an unknown option, even though JavaScript parses `-1E3` and `-1e3` identically (`Number('-1E3') === -1000`).

```js
program.argument('<temp>');
program.parse(['-1e3'], { from: 'user' }); // ok
program.parse(['-1E3'], { from: 'user' }); // error: unknown option '-1E3'
```

## Cause

In `lib/command.js`, `negativeNumberArg` tests the arg against `/^-(\d+|\d*\.\d+)(e[+-]?\d+)?$/`. The exponent group matches only lowercase `e`, so an uppercase-`E` negative fails the test, is then classified as an option, lands in the unknown list, and is reported by `unknownOption()`.

## Fix

Add the `i` flag to the pattern. The only letter in it is `e`, so the flag makes `E` and `e` both match and changes nothing else. Invalid inputs such as `-1X3`, `-0xFF` and `-1e3.0` stay rejected.

## Testing

Extended the existing parametrized `negativeNumbers` cases in `tests/negatives.test.js` with the uppercase-`E` forms. They fail on the current code (rejected as unknown option) and pass with the fix. The full suite stays green.

```js
program.helpOption('-?, --help', 'show help'); // customise
```

After the change, each snippet passes `node --check`, and `npm test` (lint, unit tests, and type checks) is green.

Fixed two invalid JavaScript snippets in the JSDoc examples for `.commandsGroup()` and `.helpOption()`.

## Summary

Add documentation warning about forward slash (`/`) argument expansion in Git Bash (MINGW64) on Windows.

Closes #2380

## Changes

- Added new section "Windows MINGW64 / Git Bash" to both English and Chinese READMEs
- Documents the MSYS2 path conversion behavior that affects slash arguments
- Provides practical workarounds for users encountering this issue

## Workarounds Documented

1. Use a different character instead of `/`
2. Double the slash: `--separator //`
3. Set `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV` environment variable
4. Quote with leading slash: `--separator '///'`

## References

- [MSYS2 Filesystem Paths Documentation](https://www.msys2.org/docs/filesystem-paths/#automatic-unix-windows-path-conversion)

body:
## Problem

Commander is written in CommonJS with shims for ESM imports and types, and a complex exports in `package.json`. It would be nice to move to ESM now that node supports `require(esm)`.

We have a relatively low overhead CommonJS implementation with the ESM shim. This also avoids the dual-package hazard. However moving forward, there will be more situations where there is friction to support CommonJS implementation in ESM-first tooling (e.g. https://github.com/tj/commander.js/issues/2345#issuecomment-3442907147). 

With `require(esm)` now available in Node.js, and Deno and Bun having supported this for some time, there is solid runtime support for ESM-only dependencies. Hurrah! A major blocker removed.

Some tooling still requires extra work for ESM, with Jest being a common example. Also a familiar example, because we were using it in Commander ourselves! To be fair on Jest, it is stuck waiting for some API issues to be worked through in Node.js, and even upstream in V8. Some popular libraries went ESM-only years ago so the work required to support ESM-only is fairly well established.

Some ESM-only related links:
- https://e18e.dev/blog/migrating-the-ecosystem-to-esm.html
- https://antfu.me/posts/move-on-to-esm-only

Packages gone ESM-only:
- https://storybook.js.org/blog/storybook-is-going-esm-only/
- https://github.com/yargs/yargs/pull/2451

See: #2345

## Solution

Go ESM-only. Document migration tips for common scenarios. Note that Commander 14 will be supported until (approximately) May 2027 so users do not need to update now. (And support for ESM-only is likely to continue to improve in the meantime making an update easier.)

- switch implementation files from CommonJS to ESM
- drop the shim files
- delete deprecated `commander/esm.mjs` entry point
- simplify exports in `package.json`
- add Migration Tips in CHANGELOG as important part of migration

ToDo:
- [x] investigate whether FORCE_COLOR still needed where was added for breakage in Jest
- [x] change `package.json` type to `module`
- [x] convert tests to ESM
- [x] convert (most) example files to ESM
- [x] convert README examples to ESM
- [x] plan for impact on legacy setups, such as CommonJS projects using Jest (familiar example since that was us!)
- [ ] are the Jest `require(esm)` examples worthwhile??
  
If we proceed with this PR:
- [x] add pinned issue announcing plan
- [x] make prerelease available after this PR lands
- [ ] update commander dependency in jest examples to prerelease version

(Note: can try out Jest examples by doing `npm pack` in Commander directory and installing the resulting tar file into example folder, to overwrite the non-existent 15.0.0.)

## ChangeLog

Changed
- *Breaking:* Migrated Commander implementation from CommonJS to pure ESM (ECMAScript Modules). This is expected to be seamless for ESM consumers, but CommonJS consumers may hit issues with tooling requiring configuration for ESM-only dependencies.
- *Breaking:* Commander 15 requires Node.js v20 or higher. To be more precise, `^20.19.0 || >=22.12.0` for `require(esm)`.

Deleted
- *Breaking:* removed deprecated export of `commander/esm.mjs`

title: Switching to esm-only

body:
## Problem

I do like writing tests using Jest, but the ESM support is _still_ experimental (relies on a Node.js experimental flag). I hit this quickly when looking at converting Commander to esm-only.
- https://jestjs.io/docs/ecmascript-modules

## Solution

The radical approach in this PR is to switch to native Node.js test runner! Zero dependencies compared with large Jest install. Fast test runner. Potential downsides are simpler API patterns and switch to `node:assert`.

The Node.js  test runner does have test coverage support but still experimental. Given we do not currently enforce coverage percentage, I don't think that is a blocker.
- https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/test.html#collecting-code-coverage

Another alternative is we could switch to vitest which has a similar API to Jest and natively supports ESM. I have not used vitest, but seems to be fast and well regarded.

## ToDo

- [x] confirm does work with ESM before going too far [only a simple check, but fine]
- [x] revisit runtime test of exports from Typescript, not achieving anything? (`ts-imports.test.js`)
- [x] compare total number of tests before/after in case some tests not recognised by runner after conversion (paranoia)
- [x] turn back on `no-undef` eslint rule (when finish conversion)
- [x] delete `.example-conversion.test.js` (when finish conversion)
- [x] reenable unit tests (when finish conversion)

## ChangeLog

- (dev) switch from Jest to `node:test` test runner
